summary.title: Taking Ownership Is The Most Effective Way to Get What You Want
summary.one_liner: Taking ownership of your own contribution to problems, rather than blaming external factors, is the most effective way to regain control and get results.
takeaways: Learned helplessness shows that believing negative events are outside your control leads to giving up, while taking ownership restores a sense of control.
Blaming external factors is the default but wastes energy; focusing on your own contribution is more effective.
Use 'How might I...?' questions to turn frustrations with other teams, managers, or processes into actions you can take.
Ownership does not mean ignoring problems; you can consciously choose not to act, but then accept the consequences.
Venting is fine, but the key question is what you will do differently within your own sphere of influence.
summary.summary: The article draws on Martin Seligman's learned helplessness experiments and Jocko Willink's concept of extreme ownership to argue that people who see themselves as responsible for what they can influence get better results than those who blame external factors. It contrasts blaming a late project on product managers or other teams with owning one's part, such as not de-risking early or not communicating changed assumptions. The author then gives practical guidance, with example prompts for handling blocked teams, micromanaging managers, and teams that ignore best practices. The post ends by asking readers to focus on what they can change.
